Write a script, named jump_analyzer.py, and place it in `/tmp/obench-cell-a3jm8hc3/bench_opencode_video-processing_mn5fk082/jump_analyzer.py` . The script analyzes MP4 videos of hurdle jumpers and extracts performance metrics. In the video, there is a single jump recorded. You have to figure out how to detect when the jump happens. The background, position of the camera, and position of the hurdle is the same in all videos.Your software should take an MP4 video file as input and output a TOML file with the exact structure and field names shown below. There's an example video for development in `/tmp/obench-cell-a3jm8hc3/bench_opencode_video-processing_mn5fk082/example_video.mp4`.

## Dependencies
You have access to toml, cv2 and numpy. You can only use these libraries.

## Input
MP4 video file of an athlete jumping over hurdles
The video is filmed with a monocular (single) camera from a stationary position
Videos show athletes running and jumping over track hurdles

## Required Output Format
Your software must generate a TOML file with exactly these fields and names, and store it in `/tmp/obench-cell-a3jm8hc3/bench_opencode_video-processing_mn5fk082/output.toml`

```toml
jump_takeoff_frame_number = [integer]
jump_land_frame_number = [integer] 
```

## Field Definitions
`jump_takeoff_frame_number`: Frame number where the athlete's takeoff/jump begins
`jump_land_frame_number`: Frame number where the athlete lands

## Constraints and Assumptions
All test videos will have the same dimensions and scale as the example provided
You can assume the first frame of the video has no runner on the track

I wrote `jump_analyzer.py`. On the example video it writes `jump_takeoff_frame_number = 54` and `jump_land_frame_number = 62` to `output.toml`. I couldn't view images here, so I haven't checked those two frames against the video by eye.

**How it works:**
- It subtracts the blurred first frame (the empty track) from every frame to isolate the runner.
- It tracks the lowest point of the runner's silhouette, which is roughly the feet.
- The jump is the stretch of consecutive frames where that point sits well above its usual ground level.
- Takeoff is the first frame in that stretch. Landing is the first frame after it, when the feet are back on the ground.

**Things to know:**
- The `toml` module isn't installed in this environment. The script falls back to writing the two lines by hand, which gives the same format.
- The takeoff frame could reasonably be counted as 53 or 54, depending on how you define "begins". I used the first frame where the feet are clearly airborne. If your reference counts the last frame on the ground, subtract 1.
- Later frames, around 110 to 117, have small bright blobs that aren't the runner. The script ignores them by only analysing the longest run of frames where a large enough figure is visible.
